Q: Token is not provided A:

either in state (memory), session storage, or local storage... or as an httponly cookie so you can set it from the backend... but you haven't shown how you consume it... probably best to use specific methods built-in to your frameworks for doing this on frontend and back. (avoid "rolling your own" security)

Q: Visual Studio debugger crashes when selecting IFormFile in Swagger UI A:

This issue might be caused by the Stop debugger when browser window is closed, close browser when debugging stops option within Visual Studio.

Essentially, when opening the file picker by Swagger, Visual Studio thinks the window has been closed and stops the debugger.

Turning the setting off fixed this issue for me.

Q: Print capture groups for every match A:

Replace for to while

... | perl -Mv5.14 -wne'say "$1-->$2" while /(\d)([a-z])/g'

With the for loop the regex is computed in a list context causing very different behavior

In particular, this is about the behavior of /g modifier in list-vs-scalar context. From perlop

The /g modifier specifies global pattern matching--that is, matching as many times as possible within the string. How it behaves depends on the context. In list context, it returns a list of the substrings matched by any capturing parentheses in the regular expression. If there are no parentheses, it returns a list of all the matched strings, as if there were parentheses around the whole pattern.

In scalar context, each execution of m//g finds the next match, returning true if it matches, and false if there is no further match. The position after the last match can be read or set using the pos() function; see "pos" in perlfunc. A failed match normally resets the search position to the beginning of the string, but you can avoid that by adding the /c modifier (for example, m//gc). Modifying the target string also resets the search position.

In the for loop's list the regex is in list context and we get back all captures -- with $1 and $2 being set to the last two, what we then get in each for-loop iteration. But the while loop sets the scalar context for its condition and then /g iterates through matches in the string so each time we get back the next pair of the specified two captures, with the corresponding $1 and $2.

  • The -Mv5.14 is there for say, as the simple -E isn't good for future. Thanks to ikegami

  • That \d is Unicode and locale aware and it matches anything that has \p{Digit} property. That's some 300-odd characters I think from various writing systems and this can be very misleading or even dangerous, if you cross paths with Unicode.

    This is constrained to ASCII by the /a modifier but why not use [0-9] if you want ASCII?

    See perlrecharclass and for instance this SO page. Also, ask AI for examples, like: perl show examples of what kinds of unicode characters does \d pattern for digits matches in a regex

Q: How to call a *.py from within Python along with a variable? A:

Rather than

import Child

which doesn't have access to the Parent.py namespace

exec(open('Child.py').read())

does get access to all variables and objects from Parent.py

Q: Select the rows with matching year from timestamp column A:

Seems unix timestamp so you could try using FROM_UNIXTIME

SELECT * FROM new_enquery WHERE FROM_UNIXTIME(publish_date, '%Y')= '2018'
